note.note:
ENT Clinical Note

Subjective:
- Presenting complaint and trigger/exposure
  • New-onset unilateral headache; no clear precipitating factor identified.  
- Symptom timeline and progression
  • Began yesterday mid-morning; gradual increase in intensity over a short period; persistent.  
- ENT symptoms
  • Throat swelling/closure sensation: none.  
  • Voice change/hoarseness: none.  
  • Dysphagia/odynophagia, drooling: none.  
  • Nasal/ocular symptoms: none.  
  • Stridor/noisy breathing, dyspnea: none.  
  • Facial/lip/tongue/uvular swelling: none.  
  • Ear or neck pain/swelling, hearing changes: none.  
- Relevant past episodes and treatments
  • First episode of this type of headache.  
  • Took one dose of ibuprofen yesterday with minimal relief.  
  • No prior ED visits or injectable therapies.  
- Allergies and current medications
  • Drug/food/environmental allergies: none reported.  
  • Medications: ibuprofen single dose yesterday (dose/route/frequency not documented); no regular prescriptions.  
- Social context
  • Lives with partner; consultation conducted in private setting.

Objective:
- Observable swelling and distribution: none reported.  
- Airway/breathing: no stridor, no respiratory distress.  
- Mental status/associated features: alert; denies dizziness or syncope.  
- Vitals and examination findings: Not recorded.  
- Accompaniment: patient alone during video visit.

Assessment:
- Working impression: New-onset unilateral throbbing headache, most consistent with primary headache disorder (probable migraine without aura).  
  Evidence: left posterior throbbing pain (8/10) with functional impairment; family history of migraine; absence of systemic or focal neurological signs.  

- Differential diagnosis (aligned with DDx)
  1. Migraine without aura – high likelihood; fits unilateral throbbing quality and family history; opposing evidence: first-ever episode and lack of nausea/photophobia.  
  2. Tension-type headache – medium likelihood; common primary headache; opposing evidence: pain is unilateral and severe.  
  3. Cervicogenic headache – medium-low likelihood; occipital location and sedentary job may contribute; opposing evidence: no neck pain or positional change.  

Plan:
- Immediate management
  • Prescribed stronger NSAID (specific agent not documented) to be taken regularly with food, not concurrently with ibuprofen.  
  • May combine with paracetamol as needed.  
- Patient instructions
  • Rest, maintain adequate hydration.  
  • Monitor symptoms closely.  
- Escalation criteria / red flags
  • Seek urgent medical review if headache worsens, develops fever, rash, vomiting, neck stiffness, visual changes, focal weakness, or recurs in similar episodes.  
- Follow-up
  • Re-contact the service within 1–2 days if no improvement after new analgesic regimen or sooner if red flags occur.  
  • Consider in-person evaluation with vitals and neurological examination if symptoms persist or recur.  

Quality checks (document_quality):
● Missing elements: objective vitals, neurological exam, detailed medication name/dose, complete allergy list, menstrual/OCP history (relevant for CVST risk), auto-injector/anaphylaxis plan (not applicable but standard ENT template element).  
● Conflicts between transcript and DDx: none identified.  
● Transcript quality: clear audio; no significant inaudible sections.
